name: Denggan
confidence_why: Hoback 2024, the only first-hand description of Denggan phonology, measured vowel duration, intensity and pitch and found penultimate prominence in isolated elicited words but no consistent word-stress pattern in connected speech, leaving stress undetermined, while Hoback 2018 and Lynch & Crowley 2001 say nothing about stress.
catalog_citation: Hoback, Brittany. 2024. A Sociolinguistic Study of Language Documentation: Denggan (Banam Bay, Malekula, Vanuatu). PhD thesis, Te Herenga Waka - Victoria University of Wellington. 450 pp. Open access:https://openaccess.wgtn.ac.nz/articles/thesis/25272091
catalog_locator: Ch. 6 grammar sketch, sec. 6.2.4.2 'Stress', pp. 224-226, and sec. 6.2.4.2.5 'Discussion of stress', pp. 230-231; tone statement sec. 6.2.4.1 p. 224
catalog_quote: Denggan seems to exhibit penultimate stress in some instances. For example, in the spectrograms below, pitch and vowel length seem to indicate stress on the penultimate syllable (Figure 13, Figure 14 and Figure 15). ... While Denggan exhibits some penultimate stress on elicited isolated words, this stress is not always consistent in connected speech. ... It is not always clear which syllable receives indicators of stress. ... Our tests using Denggan data show similar lack of predictable stress contrast based on measuring pitch, vowel length and intensity. It could be possible that stress in Denggan is more related to phrasal stress than individual stress placement on syllables with a word. It could also be that stress on syllables in Denggan were historically penultimate, but that the final syllable has been lost and the stress remained on the synchronic last syllable for some words. ... Therefore, while some words in Denggan exhibit penultimate stress, other words and phrases are less predictable for assigning stress. Consequently, determining the stress patterns in Denggan remains an avenue of further investigation.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (450 pp., text present; the PDF's metadata gives the Author = Brittany Hoback, created 2024-02-23). I extracted pp. 241-248 (printed 224-231) with extracted text and read sec. 6.2.4 'Suprasegmental phonology' in full. Every segment of the compilers quote is present verbatim at the stated locators: p. 224 'Denggan seems to exhibit penultimate stress in some instances. For example, in the spectrograms below, pitch and vowel length seem to indicate stress on the penultimate syllable (Figure 13, Figure 14 and Figure 15).'; p. 226 'While Denggan exhibits some penultimate stress on elicited isolated words, this stress is not always consistent in connected speech.'; p. 230 'Our tests…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words elicited in isolation tend to carry penultimate stress (cued by pitch and vowel duration), but in connected speech no syllable is consistently prominent; instrumental measurements (duration, intensity, F0 over di- and trisyllables, three speakers) found no predictable word-stress position, and the author leaves the system undetermined, suggesting prominence may be phrasal or, in some words, final (historically penultimate before loss of a final syllable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Denggan (only Pearce's remark on Unua primary/secondary stress is quoted for comparison).
new_statements.exceptions: Connected-speech tokens (e.g. the phrase 'at smatfe rason') show unpredictable prominence; author speculates some words keep stress on the synchronic final syllable after historical loss of an atonic final syllable (citing Charpentier 1982 Vol. 1 p. 65 on coastal South Malekula languages); initial syllable tends to be shortest/least intense.
new_statements.domain_note: Penultimate tendency explicitly restricted to elicited isolated (citation) forms; connected speech inconsistent; author raises the possibility that prominence is phrase-level rather than word-level. Language explicitly stated to be non-tonal (sec. 6.2.4.1, p. 224).
new_statements.identity_note: Hoback's thesis describes 'Denggan', the community's current name for the language formerly called Banam Bay Language / Burmbar (ISO vrt = Glottolog burm1263); she treats Tryon's Fartavo, Lepaxivir/Repaxivir and Burmbar village lists as one language (thesis p. 6). Data from Banam Bay villages, SE Malekula, 2016-2019 fieldwork. Same languoid as the target; no dialect restriction beyond minor village variation.

sources.note: Sec. 6.2.4.2 (pp. 224-231): elicited isolated words often show penultimate stress (spectrograms of brahas 'cold', garen 'tail-3SG'), but stress is not consistent in connected speech; instrumental plots of vowel duration, intensity and pitch across three speakers show no predictable stressed syllable; author suggests stress may be phrasal, or final in some words after historical loss of final syllables; concludes stress remains undetermined. Also states Denggan is not tonal (6.2.4.1).
